title: Hollow Diamond Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: gap-and-edge per-cell checks versus measuring each row by its distance from the nearest tip and building its edges directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer n, print the outline of a diamond with 2n minus 1 rows, where only the two slanted edges of every row are stars, and everything between them, including the widest middle row, is a space.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print the outline of a diamond with 2n minus 1 rows, where only the two slanted edges of every row are stars, and everything between them, including the widest middle row, is a space.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Diamond Shaped Wire Frame
blocks.text: Picture a diamond shape bent entirely out of thin wire, with nothing filling the inside, not even at its widest point in the middle. Every row is just the two points where that wire frame crosses it, with empty space everywhere in between.

blocks.caption: Only the first and last position of every row are stars, even at the widest point

This shape looks like it needs entirely new reasoning, but it is worth checking how much of it can be assembled directly from the two closely related problems already solved earlier in this division.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The distance-from-nearest-tip measurement, m equal to min of r and 2n minus r, is exactly the same idea already used for the solid diamond, and it still correctly folds both the widening and narrowing halves into one shared value.

Observation 2: The edge-only row construction, a star, a hollow gap, and a star, is exactly the same idea already used for the hollow pyramid's ordinary rows.

Observation 3: The one genuine difference from the hollow pyramid is that there is no flat base here, a diamond has two single-point tips, not a solid foundation, so unlike the hollow pyramid, no row is ever a special, fully solid case, not even the widest middle row.

Observation 4: So this shape needs no new construction technique at all, it is simply the diamond's distance measurement combined with the pyramid's hollow-edge row shape, applied uniformly to every single row.

Explicitly noting that missing special case, no solid row anywhere, is exactly the kind of detail that separates a shallow copy-paste from a solution that shows real understanding of what changed between two related problems.

For every row, first work out its distance from the nearer tip, then check every column individually, printing a space while still in the leading gap, a star at the first or last position of the star region, and a space everywhere else in between.

items: Loop over every row r, from 1 to 2n minus 1.
Compute m, the distance of this row from whichever tip is closer.
Compute the gap, n minus m, and the star region width, 2m minus 1.
For each column, print a space while still in the gap.
Once past the gap, print a star only at the first or last position of the star region, and a space everywhere else in between.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: find the distance from the nearest tip, then check gap and edge per column

codes.python:
def hollow_diamond(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):          # r counts every row, top tip to bottom tip
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)                     # this row's distance from the nearest tip
        gap = n - m
        width = 2 * m - 1
        for j in range(gap + width):               # check every column this row actually uses
            if j < gap:
                print(" ", end="")                    # still inside the leading gap
                continue
            k = j - gap                             # position inside the star region
            if k == 0 or k == width - 1:
                print("*", end="")                    # left or right edge of this row
            else:
                print(" ", end="")                    # interior of this row stays hollow
        print()                                    # move to the next line after the row


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hollow_diamond(4)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: m is computed once per row exactly as with the solid diamond, folding both the widening and narrowing halves into one shared distance value.
gap and width are derived from m using the same formulas as the hollow pyramid's ordinary rows, n minus m and 2m minus 1, applied here to every row with no exception for the widest one.
The edge check, k equal to 0 or k equal to width minus 1, is still re-evaluated once per column, even though only two specific positions in the row will ever be stars.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every row correctly measures its distance from the nearer tip, and every column within that row is checked against both the gap and the edge condition.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total width across the full diamond outline is proportional to n squared, and every position gets its own check.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: once the gap and width for a row are known, checking every interior column one at a time is unnecessary, since only the first and last position of the star region ever hold a star. That entire region can be built directly in one operation, without visiting each position individually.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: once m and the resulting width are known for a row, checking every interior position for whether it is the first or last one repeats a decision that only ever has two true outcomes per row.

What stays the same as two earlier problems: the distance measurement from the solid diamond, and the edge-only row construction from the hollow pyramid, both transfer here completely unchanged.

What is different here: there is no special solid row, since a diamond's tips are single points rather than a flat base, every row, including the widest one, follows the exact same hollow-edge rule.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, a star, a gap of spaces, and a star, or just a single star when the width is only 1, builds each row's star region in one or two operations.

The core idea: compute m once per row, then build the hollow star region directly from it, with no special case for any row, not even the widest one.

For each row, compute its distance from the nearer tip once, then build the leading gap directly, and build the star region as either a single star, when the row is only one star wide, or a star, a gap of spaces, and a star otherwise. Concatenate both pieces and print the row with a single call.
For each row, compute its distance from the nearer tip once, then build the hollow star region directly and print the whole row with a single call.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: find the distance from the nearest tip, build the row directly

codes.python:
def hollow_diamond(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):          # r counts every row, top tip to bottom tip
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)                     # this row's distance from the nearest tip
        gap = n - m
        width = 2 * m - 1
        stars = "*" if width == 1 else "*" + " " * (width - 2) + "*"  # only the two edges, direct
        row = " " * gap + stars
        print(row)                               # one print call per row instead of per character


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hollow_diamond(4)

blocks.text: This works because m still correctly measures every row's distance from the nearer tip, exactly as with the solid diamond, and because a row's hollow star region depends only on its width, exactly as with the hollow pyramid's ordinary rows; since a diamond has no flat base, that same hollow-edge construction applies uniformly to every single row, including the widest one, with no special case anywhere.

The star region is built as either a single star or a star-gap-star construction depending only on width, reusing the hollow pyramid's ordinary-row logic for every row with no exception.
Concatenating the leading gap and the star region and printing once per row completes the entire hollow diamond without ever special casing the widest row.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

codes.python:
def hollow_diamond(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    rows = []
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)
        gap = n - m
        width = 2 * m - 1
        stars = "*" if width == 1 else "*" + " " * (width - 2) + "*"
        rows.append(" " * gap + stars)              # build every row directly, one operation each
    print("\n".join(rows))                        # join every row and output the whole pattern at once


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hollow_diamond(4)

items: Every row is still built directly from its own m and width, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is collecting each finished row instead of printing it immediately.
Joining all 2n minus 1 rows with newline characters assembles the complete hollow diamond as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole outline, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: A hollow diamond combines the edge only row logic from a hollow pyramid with the distance from the nearest tip idea from a solid diamond, but unlike the hollow pyramid, there is no special solid row anywhere, since a diamond has no flat base, both tips are single points and the shape is symmetric all the way through.

items: Copying the hollow pyramid solution directly and accidentally making the widest middle row solid, when it should stay hollow like every other row.
Forgetting that a width of 1 star has no interior to hollow out, and would otherwise produce an empty string.
Getting the distance from the nearest tip formula wrong, which breaks the symmetry between the top and bottom halves.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how is this different from the hollow pyramid", think: a diamond has two point tips instead of a flat base, so no row is ever a special, fully solid case.
If the interviewer says "can you reuse work from an earlier problem", think: combine the diamond's distance measurement with the pyramid's hollow-edge row construction directly.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: gap-and-edge per cell checks in the brute force version, one formula built row per print call in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: hollow shape printing that combines the edge-only row construction from the hollow pyramid with the distance-from-nearest-tip measurement from the solid diamond, but with no special solid row anywhere.

Core Idea: compute m, a row's distance from the nearer tip, exactly as with the solid diamond, then build that row's hollow star region, a single star or a star-gap-star, exactly as with the hollow pyramid's ordinary rows, applied uniformly with no special case for any row.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: combining two previously solved techniques often works directly, but only after carefully checking whether any special case from either original problem still applies.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape by adapting the hollow pyramid; explicitly noting the missing special row is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: diamond's distance measurement plus pyramid's hollow-edge row, but with no solid row anywhere.
